query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrMnFeCoNi‐type high-entropy alloys, toughness retention at intermediate temperatures is governed by an interplay between two competing near‐grain-boundary mechanisms: (1) a deleterious rapid nanosegregation of principal elements at the grain boundaries that reduces cohesion and promotes intergranular cracking, and (2) a beneficial deformation‐induced crystalline‐to‐amorphous transformation that forms nanoscale amorphous bridges at crack tips, which shield them from propagation. By pre‐engineering the grain boundary chemistry (for example, via controlled heat treatment to promote preexisting Cr-rich secondary precipitates), the embrittling effect of fast nanosegregation can be mitigated, thereby allowing the amorphous nanobridge formation to dominate and preserve toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy with standard (as-solidified or conventionally heat-treated) grain boundaries that are susceptible to rapid principal-element nanosegregation at intermediate temperatures.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat-treatment protocol designed to induce preexisting Cr-rich secondary precipitates (a form of grain boundary segregation engineering) prior to mechanical testing.
generation.conditions: Testing under controlled intermediate temperatures (e.g., ~500–700°C) and strain rates typical for service loading; the intervention and baseline alloys should be processed under identical conditions aside from the segregation-engineering heat treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary chemistry, particularly the presence or absence of preformed Cr-rich precipitates, which mediates whether fast nanosegregation occurs and, consequently, whether near-crack deformation can promote amorphous nanobridge formation.
generation.mechanism: In the untreated alloy, rapid nanosegregation of elements like Cr, Ni, and Mn at grain boundaries weakens cohesion, leading to intergranular cracking and toughness loss. In contrast, when grain boundary chemistry is pre-engineered via controlled heat-treatment to produce Cr-rich precipitates, the fast segregation of embrittling elements is curtailed. This allows the high local stresses at a propagating crack tip to trigger a controlled crystalline-to-amorphous transformation which produces nanoscale amorphous bridges that shield the crack and enhance toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the segregation-engineered sample will display an increased incidence and continuity of amorphous nanobridges in the crack-tip region (observed in situ via TEM) and a measurable improvement in fracture toughness and ductility at intermediate temperatures.
generation.baseline: The untreated alloy exhibiting grain boundaries prone to fast nanosegregation that lead to intergranular cracking and a lower measured toughness at intermediate temperatures.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to single-phase, fcc CrMnFeCoNi-type high-entropy alloys under intermediate temperature (500–700°C) and moderate strain rate conditions typical of engineering applications; effects at very low (cryogenic) or extremely high temperatures, or in alloys with very different chemistries or microstructures, might not follow the same balance.
generation.uncertainty: The interplay between the beneficial amorphous nanobridge formation (as reported in PMC8011962::web::022::discussion) and the deleterious grain boundary nanosegregation leading to embrittlement (PMC6897545::web::012::gb_segregation_engineering_to_enhance_du) has not been quantitatively established. The proposed intervention extends these independent findings by directly testing how pre-engineering the GB chemistry shifts the balance between these opposing mechanisms.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrMnFeCoNi HEA samples: one set processed with a controlled heat treatment to induce Cr-rich precipitates at the grain boundaries (segregation-engineered group) and an otherwise identical set processed with a conventional heat treatment (baseline group). Perform standardized intermediate-temperature tensile and fracture toughness tests while using in situ TEM to observe crack-tip microstructural evolution.
measurements: Fracture toughness (e.g., K_Ic) and tensile ductility measurements at ~500–700°C
High-resolution TEM imaging of crack-tip regions to assess the presence, continuity, and morphology of amorphous nanobridges
Chemical mapping (e.g., via APT or EDS) of grain boundaries to quantify the extent of elemental segregation in both groups
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the segregation-engineered samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in amorphous bridge formation at crack tips and fail to show improved fracture toughness and ductility compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis—that pre-engineered grain boundaries favor a transition to beneficial amorphous nanobridge formation over deleterious nanosegregation—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Although the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is lower than the single-phase HEA at the testing temperature below 500°C, the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is greater than the single-phase HEA at 600° and 700°C. No intergranular embrittlement is observed. Figure 5 (B and C) shows the lateral surface in the vicinity of the fracture after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. Figure 5 (D and E) exhibits typical ductile dimples on fracture surfaces after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. In contrast to single-phase samples (Fig. 3D), the dual-phase sample has very few cracks near the lateral fracture surface. This suggests that the GB segregation engineering strategy via preexisting Cr-rich precipitates is effective to evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures in HEAs. This is because the embrittling elements—such as Cr, Mn, or Ni—can be absorbed by preexisting embrittling element–enriched precipitates at GBs, which only leads to the growth of precipitates rather than GB embrittlement. While strength and ductility are the global mechanical properties controlled by their bulk responses, fracture toughness originates from the resistance to crack initiation and propagation that is more closely related to the local microstructure and evolution. Therefore, the near-tip mechanisms revealed in this work, including the crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation and formation of amorphous nanobridges, could be generally applicable to the toughening of other UFG HEAs. In conclusion, we have found the deformation-induced crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation in the UFG Cantor alloy. The structural evolution exhibits a sequence of formation of the crystalline, lamellar, spotted, and amorphous patterns in TEM images that arise from different proportions and organizations of the crystalline and amorphous structures. The crack-tip high stresses, high lattice and grain boundary resistances to dislocation slip, and resulting accumulation of high-density dislocations are essential to the observed solid-state amorphization, thereby dissipating energy and resisting crack propagation.
